newsitem.title: USA: Commission censures Illinois Supreme Court justice.
newsitem.headline: Commission censures Illinois Supreme Court justice.

text.p: A judicial commission voted Wednesday to censure the chief justice of the Illinois Supreme Court for what it said was direputable behaviour when he was stopped for traffic violations.

The five-member Illinois Courts Commission unanimously agreed to censure Chief Justice James Heiple, a stiffer penalty than a reprimand but not as severe as the suspension or removal from the bench that Heiple's critics had sought.
Heiple is also the object of a separate impeachment proceeding in the state legislature.

The members of the commission, which included a chairman hand-picked by Heiple himself, wrote that he violated Supreme Court rules and it "further determined that (his) conduct was prejudicial to the administration of justice and brought the judicial office into disrepute."

Heiple, who was elected in January by his six fellow justices to head the state's highest court for the next three years, issued a statement after the ruling saying he was disappointed by the commission's decision but accepted it, and he apologised to the police and public.

The commission held a hearing earlier this month for Heiple at which he did not dispute the facts of the case, precluding the appearance of any witnesses for or against him. After the hearing, he defended his actions to reporters and complained that the police had treated him roughly, demonstrating how he was flung across the hood of his car.

Heiple was arrested after he allegedly ignored an order to stop his car. Other police officers later alleged that they had stopped him in the past for traffic offences but that he had flashed his court credentials and been allowed to go free.

He has also been criticised for some controversial opinions, most notably one involving "Baby Richard," a Chicago-area child who was returned to his natural parents years after his birth mother had given him up for adoption.
Illinois Lt. Gov. Bob Kustra said Wednesday's decision showed that Heiple was guilty of "an arrogance of power that has led to a crisis of confidence in our state's highest court."
He said he hoped the move would encourage Heiple to resign from the court.
